title: Stonehenge Altar Stone: Origin Still a Mystery
paragraphs: Few objects at Stonehenge are as quietly enigmatic as the Altar Stone, a six-ton slab of sandstone about 4.9 metres long. For nearly a century the prevailing wisdom held that it came from west Wales, like the smaller bluestones, which travelled some 225 kilometres. Subsequent work then pointed towards north-east Scotland, an origin that would have demanded a considerably longer journey for a Neolithic community.

That conclusion has now been scrutinised by a team led by Professor Duncan Pirrie of the University of South Wales, whose paper appears in the Journal of the Geological Society. The researchers paired new observations of the monument with analyses of fragments preserved in museum collections, assembling a geological fingerprint from the rock's structure, mineralogy, geochemistry and isotopic signature, and measuring it against formations across Britain, notably those of Scotland's Orcadian Basin.

The findings are sobering rather than conclusive. "So far, none of the locations examined have the same set of characteristics as the Altar Stone," Pirrie observed. Several candidate sources have been ruled out, yet a Scottish origin has not been disproved, and the stone's provenance stays undetermined. The authors' stance is pragmatic: each location eliminated narrows the field and brings the search closer to its goal.

questions.q: What did the new study set out to do?
questions.a: Test the idea that the stone came from Scotland.
The place where the stone originally came from.

questions.q: Why is the finding described as 'sobering rather than conclusive'?
questions.a: It rules out places but does not identify the real source.
